claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy is in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution state with a disordered FCC/BCC-type structure.
Slow annealing promotes diffusional nucleation and ordered growth of nanoscale intermetallic precipitates.
The nanoscale intermetallic precipitates form or promote a uniform protective passive layer.
The precipitate-associated passive layer enhances corrosion resistance.
The precipitate-associated passive or oxide layer enhances high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Rapid quenching suppresses the proposed intermetallic transformation.
Rapid quenching leaves an unstable or underdeveloped passivation layer.
The proposed controlled comparison is a slow-ramp anneal with varied ramp rates and dwell durations versus rapid quenching from the service-temperature regime.
Annealing is proposed over an intermediate temperature window of 500–600 °C, followed by quenching.
The treated samples are to be exposed to oxidizing service conditions at 600–700 °C.
The structural mediator consists of nanoscale Mg–Zn- or Mg–Ti-based intermetallic compounds emerging through solute segregation.
Enhanced atomic diffusion during slow annealing facilitates intermetallic nucleation and controlled growth.
Intermetallic precipitates modify local surface chemistry so as to stabilize a protective film against corrosion and oxidation.
Slow-annealed samples will contain a more uniform distribution of finely dispersed intermetallic precipitates than rapidly quenched samples.
Slow-annealed samples will form more robust passivating oxide layers than rapidly quenched samples.
Slow-annealed samples will exhibit greater electrochemical corrosion resistance and lower oxidation rates than rapidly quenched samples.
The proposed mechanism is expected to operate at service temperatures of 600–700 °C if complete phase separation and excessive grain growth are avoided.
The initial metastable state has limited precipitation and variable, potentially unstable passivation behavior in oxidizing environments.
The kinetic thresholds, relevant local-composition effects, and optimal dwell times and ramp rates are not yet known.

Failure of slow annealing to produce a statistically significant increase in fine, uniformly distributed precipitates together with a more protective film and improved corrosion or oxidation performance would falsify the proposed mechanism.
